1.pericope_label: the law of the leper, and the priest who goes out to him

schools.summary: Ellicott notes that this law goes to Moses alone where the law of detection went to Moses and Aaron, and has the man conducted to an appointed place on the border; Keil and Delitzsch read the first act as restoring a man reckoned dead to the living members of the covenant nation.

Calvin holds that God keeps the honour of the cure to himself while giving the priest a real office — the minister proclaims a sentence already passed, yet the man who testifies that we are reconciled truly takes away our pollution; Gill has the law given to Moses for delivery to Aaron's house.
Henry infers from the existence of a cleansing law that the disease was not incurable, and finds the mercy in priests being sent to a man who could not come to them.

Wesley distinguishes the real healing, which is God's, from the declarative cleansing, which is the priest's; Clarke notes that without the priest's word there was no readmission to civil or religious society.

themes: the priest goes forth out of the camp
healed by God, pronounced clean by the priest
restoration to the congregation

4.pericope_label: two birds, cedar, scarlet and hyssop

schools.summary: Ellicott supplies the second-Temple specifications for each of the four materials, the construction of the sprinkler, and the rule of a new vessel and living water; he makes the release of the bird a picture of the man's restored liberty.
Gill reports three opinions about where the sprinkling fell — the veil over the face, the back of the hand, the forehead.
Henry reads the slain and living birds as Christ dying for our sins and rising for our justification, and the upward flight as a charge not to spend the restored life on earthly things.

Clarke describes the aspergillum made of the four materials and warns that running analogies between type and antitype is precarious; Wesley matches cedar, scarlet and hyssop to soundness, colour and the removal of the smell.

outliers: Ellicott passes on an older tradition inverting the usual symbolism: the cedar, as the loftiest tree, stands for the haughtiness that called the affliction down, and the hyssop for the humility without which it cannot be cured.
themes: the bird killed over running water in an earthen vessel
sprinkled seven times and pronounced clean
the living bird let loose into the open field

8.pericope_label: washing, shaving, and the seven days

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch divide the ritual at the seventh day, the second act restoring fellowship with God and access to the sanctuary; Ellicott would render the last clause as bathing, objects that one ritual phrase is translated three ways, and denies that the washing disinfects anything.
Gill has the clothes washed so that no remains of the infection and no ill scent should be carried to others.
Henry marks the gap between being pronounced clean and making oneself clean, and applies it to those who have the comfort of remission.
Clarke's reason for the shaving is that the water might reach every part; Wesley's is that the soundness could be seen and nothing left in which the disease might lurk.

debates.question: Was the seclusion hygienic or ceremonial?
positions: Ellicott: the disease was not contagious, and the washing is an act of purification
Wesley: he stays out of his tent lest leprosy still lurking in him infect his family

outliers: Ellicott passes on the second-Temple reading of the week outside the tent as a euphemism for abstinence, the Chaldee paraphrase making it explicit.
themes: shave off all his hair and wash in water
seven days outside his own tent
the second washing on the seventh day

10.pericope_label: the eighth day, and the offerings brought to the door

schools.summary: Ellicott explains the unusual triple meat offering as standing in for the drink offering the expiatory sacrifices would have carried, notes that the log occurs nowhere else in the Hebrew scriptures, and places the man at the gate of Nicanor; Keil and Delitzsch note that the trespass offering was most holy and the priest's.

Calvin makes the eighth day a second birth, the sacrifice renewing a circumcision in some measure effaced, and then refuses to explain the details he cannot account for; Gill describes the hands laid on the victim through the gate.
Henry reads the presentation as an obligation of gratitude and urges taking the first opportunity to use restored access to the ordinances.

Clarke assigns each offering its function — impurity, transgression, thanksgiving; Wesley ascribes the healing to God and the cleansing to the priest, and finds in the trespass offering the teaching that sin caused the disease.

themes: two he lambs, one ewe lamb, flour and a log of oil
presented before the LORD at the door
the trespass offering waved

14.pericope_label: blood and oil on the ear, the thumb and the toe

schools.summary: Ellicott reconstructs the whole procedure from second-Temple practice — two priests, two portions of blood, the man reaching through the gate — and reports that the oil on the head was held to effect the atonement; Keil and Delitzsch explain the first sevenfold sprinkling as consecrating the oil.
Gill gives the same account of the two priests and the two portions of the blood.
Henry, quoting Bishop Patrick, makes the blood a token of forgiveness and the oil of healing, and observes that the oil lies on the blood as the water had blood in it.
Wesley reads the three points as the restoration of ordinary use — to hear, to touch, to go where one pleases — and pairs blood with remission and oil with renewal.

themes: the tip of the right ear, the thumb, the great toe
oil sprinkled seven times before the LORD
the remnant of the oil upon his head

19.pericope_label: the sin offering and the burnt offering

schools.summary: Ellicott confines the sin offering to the sins committed during the illness — probably impatient words — rather than to the state of uncleanness itself, and marks the burnt offering as the terminus of the second stage; Keil and Delitzsch note that expiation could not begin until everything else had been done.
Gill identifies the ewe lamb by the ordinary rite of the sin offering and raises the question of which offering the three tenth deals accompanied.
Henry finds two things in the repeated formula of atonement — moral guilt pardoned and ceremonial pollution removed — and reads the burnt offering as thanksgiving.

themes: atonement for him that is to be cleansed
the burnt offering and the meat offering
and he shall be clean

21.pericope_label: the provision for the poor man

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch note that the burnt and sin offerings are reduced but the trespass offering is not, being the condition of reinstatement in full covenant rights; Ellicott lists what remains and points out that the first stage is not reduced at all.

Calvin infers that sacrifices are valued not at their intrinsic worth but by the disposition that offers in proportion to what a man has; Gill records the further indulgence that the best bird a man could get was accepted.
Henry insists that poverty excuses no one from bringing anything, and that the identical ceremony was performed over the meaner sacrifice because the souls are as precious.
Clarke holds that there could be no cleansing without a sacrifice, so even the poor man must find his lamb.

themes: if he be poor, and cannot get so much
two turtledoves or two young pigeons
the same ceremony over a meaner sacrifice

33.pericope_label: the plague in a house, and who sends it

schools.summary: Ellicott counts this the first of four laws in the book given prospectively, reports the second-Temple ruling that the plague was peculiar to Palestine and unknown in Jerusalem, and explains the tentative formula the owner had to use.

Calvin takes the house-plague as a severer penalty fitting a people honoured with greater privileges, and reads the required confession as a training in purity; Gill notes that Israel was in tents and the law could not yet take effect.
Henry warns that a place in the visible church secures nobody, and that masters of families should fear the first appearance of sin at home.
Clarke resists the inference that the disease was inflicted directly, scripture often representing God as doing what he only permits, and suspects animalcula.

debates.question: Was house-leprosy supernatural or natural?
positions: Ellicott: supernatural, proceeding from the immediate hand of God
Clarke: naturally caused and only permitted, the infection probably from animalcula

outliers: The Chaldee paraphrase, reported by Ellicott, makes the plague the specific punishment of a man who built his house with stolen materials.
themes: I put the plague of leprosy in a house
it seemeth to me there is as it were a plague
a law given before the land was entered

36.pericope_label: the house emptied, examined and shut up

schools.summary: Ellicott calls the clearing a benign provision to save the household goods and argues from it that the law did not treat the disease as infectious; Keil and Delitzsch reason from the same detail that the defilement was symbolic, nothing becoming unclean until the priest had spoken.
Gill describes the scope of the clearing and reads the shutting of the door as a declaration that the house is unfit to live in.
Wesley infers from the timing of the defilement how great a difference God makes between sins of ignorance and sins against knowledge, and offers three accounts of the institution itself.

themes: empty the house before the priest goes in
hollow strakes, greenish or reddish
shut up seven days

fidelity.note: One clause extends Ellicott's argument rather than reporting it: he says the clearing shows the law did not regard leprosy as infectious, and the summary adds that a real infection would hardly have been let out of the door ahead of the inspection. The inference is his; the sharpening of it is the summary's.

39.pericope_label: stones taken out, and the house broken down

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch describe the disposal of stones and scraped dust outside the town and call the returning plague a malicious leprosy; Ellicott grades the defilement contracted by entering, sleeping or eating in a house under quarantine.
Gill has the stones drawn rather than knocked out so as not to bring the building down, never fewer than two, and reports the opinion that the owner pulled the house down himself.

Henry likens the removal to cutting off a gangrened limb, and reads the demolition as the end of an obstinate leprosy of sin in families and churches — and of the corruption that outlasts all our scraping until the earthly house is taken down.
Clarke sets out the whole timetable of the three weeks and applies the demolition to a man who wastes the means of his own conversion.

themes: take away the stones in which the plague is
he shall break down the house
he that lieth or eateth in the house shall wash his clothes

48.pericope_label: the cleansing of a healed house

schools.summary: Ellicott gives the criterion for pronouncing the house clean, the same used for men and garments; Keil and Delitzsch explain why a building needs expiation at all — sin spreads from a man to the things he handles and inhabits.
Gill refers the whole rite back to the cleansing of a leprous man and records the uncertainty about who performed it.
Henry, following Bishop Patrick, holds that the house was smitten for the owner's sake, and that Israelite houses were to be kept fit for the service of God.
Clarke calls the released bird a scape-bird on the model of the scapegoat, and argues that the rite never healed the leper but declared him healed.

outliers: Henry passes on a reading of the whole institution as typical of the idolatry that clung to the Jewish church, scraped at by the reforming kings and cured only by the captivity.
themes: two birds, cedar wood, scarlet and hyssop, for the house
the living bird let go out of the city
make an atonement for the house

54.pericope_label: this is the law of leprosy

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch treat the four verses as a single formula closing both chapters; Ellicott takes the last clause as instruction against the time when the people would have to administer these cases in the land.
Gill runs through the recapitulated list — the body, the scall, the garment, the house, and the three signs in the skin.
Henry notes that the law pertained to Israel alone, Naaman never having been sent to a priest, and makes that a lesson about the limits of church discipline.
Wesley reads the closing clause as tying the priest to plain rules the people could discern as well as he could.

debates.question: What does "to teach" govern?
positions: Ellicott: instruction for the time when the cases would have to be judged in the land
the ancient authorities and the Chaldee: instruction about which days a plague may be inspected on

themes: this is the law for all manner of plague of leprosy
to teach when it is unclean, and when it is clean
those that are without God judgeth
